{{Short description|Mathematical expression with disputed status}}
{{use dmy dates|date=July 2021|cs1-dates=y}}

'''Zero to the power of zero''', denoted as {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}}, is a [[mathematical expression]] with different interpretations depending on the context. In certain areas of mathematics, such as [[combinatorics]] and [[algebra]], {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup>}} is defined as 1 because this simplifies many [[formula]]s and ensures consistency in operations involving [[exponents]]. For instance, defining {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}} aligns with the interpretation of choosing 0 elements from a [[set (mathematics)|set]] and simplifies [[Polynomial expansion|polynomial]] and [[binomial expansions]].

In other contexts, particularly in [[mathematical analysis]], {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup>}} is often considered an [[indeterminate form]]. This is because the value of {{math|''x''{{i sup|''y''}}}} as both {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} approach 0 can lead to different results based on the [[Limit process|limiting process]]. The expression arises in limit problems and may result in a range of values or diverge to [[infinity]], making it difficult to assign a single consistent value in these cases.

The treatment of {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup>}} varies across different [[computer programming language]]s and [[software]]. While many follow the convention {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}, others leave it [[Undefined (mathematics)|undefined]] or return errors, depending on the context.

==Discrete exponents==
Many widely used formulas involving [[natural number|natural-number]] exponents require {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} to be defined as {{math|1}}.  For example, the following three interpretations of {{math|''b''{{sup|0}}}} make just as much sense for {{math|1=''b'' = 0}} as they do for positive integers {{mvar|b}}:
* The interpretation of {{math|''b''{{sup|0}}}} as an [[empty product]] assigns it the value {{math|1}}.
* The [[Exponentiation#Combinatorial interpretation|combinatorial interpretation]] of {{math|''b''<sup>0</sup>}} is the number of [[tuple|0-tuples]] of elements from a {{math|''b''}}-element set; there is exactly one 0-tuple.
* The [[Exponentiation#Powers of sets|set-theoretic interpretation]] of {{math|''b''<sup>0</sup>}} is the number of [[function (mathematics)|functions]] from the [[empty set]] to a {{math|''b''}}-element set; there is exactly one such function, namely, the [[empty function]].<ref name="Bourbaki" />
All three of these specialize to give {{math|1=0{{sup|0}} = 1}}.

==Polynomials and power series==
When evaluating [[polynomial]]s, it is convenient to define {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} as {{math|1}}.  A (real) polynomial is an expression of the form {{math|''a''<sub>0</sub>''x''<sup>0</sup> + ⋅⋅⋅ + ''a''<sub>''n''</sub>''x''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, where {{math|''x''}} is an indeterminate, and the coefficients {{math|''a''<sub>''i''</sub>}} are [[real number]]s.  Polynomials are added termwise, and multiplied by applying the [[distributive law]] and the usual rules for exponents.  With these operations, polynomials form a [[polynomial ring|ring]] {{math|'''R'''[''x'']}}.  The [[multiplicative identity]] of {{math|'''R'''[''x'']}} is the polynomial {{math|''x''<sup>0</sup>}}; that is, {{math|''x''<sup>0</sup>}} times any polynomial {{math|''p''(''x'')}} is just {{math|''p''(''x'')}}.<ref name="Bourbaki_1970_1" />  Also, polynomials can be evaluated by specializing {{math|''x''}} to a real number.  More precisely, for any given real number {{math|''r''}}, there is a unique unital [[algebra homomorphism|{{math|'''R'''}}-algebra homomorphism]] {{math|ev<sub>''r''</sub> : '''R'''[''x''] → '''R'''}} such that {{math|1=ev<sub>''r''</sub>(''x'') = ''r''}}.  Because {{math|ev<sub>''r''</sub>}} is unital, {{math|1=ev<sub>''r''</sub>(''x''<sup>0</sup>) = 1}}.  That is, {{math|1=''r''<sup>0</sup> = 1}} for each real number {{math|''r''}}, including 0.  The same argument applies with {{math|'''R'''}} replaced by any [[ring (mathematics)|ring]].<ref name="Bourbaki_1970_2" />

Defining {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}} is necessary for many polynomial identities.  For example, the [[binomial theorem]] <math display="inline">(1+x)^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{k}</math> holds for {{math|1=''x'' = 0}} only if {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}.<ref name="T4n3B" />

Similarly, rings of [[power series]] require {{math|1=''x''<sup>0</sup>}} to be defined as 1 for all specializations of {{math|''x''}}.  For example, identities like <math display="inline">\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n</math> and <math display="inline">e^x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!}</math> hold for {{math|1=''x'' = 0}} only if {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}.<ref name="8sCon" />

In order for the polynomial {{math|''x''<sup>0</sup>}} to define a [[continuous function]] {{math|'''R''' → '''R'''}}, one must define {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}.

In [[differential calculus|calculus]], the [[power rule]] <math display="inline">\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}</math> is valid for {{math|1=''n'' = 1}} at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}} only if {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}.

==Continuous exponents==
[[Image:X^y.png|right|thumb|upright=1.4|Plot of {{math|1=''z'' = ''x''{{i sup|''y''}}}}. The red curves (with {{math|''z''}} constant) yield different limits as {{math|(''x'', ''y'')}} approaches {{math|(0, 0)}}. The green curves (of finite constant slope, {{math|1=''y'' = ''ax''}}) all yield a limit of {{math|1}}.]]

Limits involving [[algebraic operation]]s can often be evaluated by replacing subexpressions with their limits; if the resulting expression does not determine the original limit, the expression is known as an [[indeterminate form]].<ref name="TUZ95" /> The expression {{math|0{{sup|0}}}} is an indeterminate form: Given real-valued functions {{math|''f''(''t'')}} and {{math|''g''(''t'')}} approaching {{math|0}} (as {{math|''t''}} approaches a real number or {{math|±∞}}) with {{math|''f''(''t'') > 0}}, the limit of {{math|''f''(''t'')<sup>''g''(''t'')</sup>}} can be any non-negative real number or {{math|+∞}}, or it can [[limit (mathematics)|diverge]], depending on {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}}. For example, each limit below involves a function {{math|''f''(''t'')<sup>''g''(''t'')</sup>}} with {{math|''f''(''t''), ''g''(''t'') → 0}} as {{math|''t'' → 0<sup>+</sup>}} (a [[one-sided limit]]), but their values are different:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\lim_{t \to 0^+} {t}^{t} &= 1 , \\
\lim_{t \to 0^+} \left(e^{-1/t^2}\right)^t &= 0, \\
\lim_{t \to 0^+} \left(e^{-1/t^2}\right)^{-t} &= +\infty, \\
\lim_{t \to 0^+} \left(a^{-1/t}\right)^{-t} &= a.
\end{align}</math>

Thus, the two-variable function {{math|''x''{{i sup|''y''}}}}, though continuous on the set {{math|{(''x'', ''y'') : ''x'' > 0}{{null}}}}, [[Classification of discontinuities#Essential discontinuity|cannot be extended]] to a [[continuous function]] on {{math|{(''x'', ''y'') : ''x'' > 0} ∪ {(0, 0)}{{null}}}}, no matter how one chooses to define {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}}.<ref name="Cbfum" />

On the other hand, if {{math|''f''}} and {{math|''g''}} are [[analytic functions]] on an open neighborhood of a number {{mvar|c}}, then {{math|''f''(''t'')<sup>''g''(''t'')</sup> → 1}} as {{mvar|t}} approaches {{mvar|c}} from any side on which {{mvar|f}} is positive.<ref name="Möbius1834" />
This and more general results can be obtained by studying the limiting behavior of the function <math display="inline">\log(f(t)^{g(t)})=g(t)\log f(t)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1      = Baxley
| first1     = John V.

| issue      = 6
| pages      = 484–486
| doi        = 10.2307/2320074 
| jstor = 2320074
| access-date = 23 November 2021
| url-access= subscription
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1      = Xiao
| first1     = Jinsen
| last2      = He

==Complex exponents==
In the [[complex domain]], the function {{math|''z''{{i sup|''w''}}}} may be defined for nonzero {{math|''z''}} by choosing a [[complex logarithm#Branches of the complex logarithm|branch]] of {{math|log ''z''}} and defining {{math|''z''{{i sup|''w''}}}} as {{math|''e''{{i sup|''w'' log ''z''}}}}. This does not define {{math|0<sup>''w''</sup>}} since there is no branch of {{math|log ''z''}} defined at {{math|1=''z'' = 0}}, let alone in a neighborhood of {{math|0}}.<ref name="04zJ8" /><ref name="W1ue5" /><ref name="rYFno" />

==History==

===As a value===
In 1752, [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] in ''[[Introductio in analysin infinitorum]]'' wrote that {{math|1=''a''{{sup|0}} = 1}}<ref name="Euler" /> and explicitly mentioned that {{math|1=0{{sup|0}} = 1}}.<ref name="UzqFL" /> An annotation attributed<ref name="Libri1833" /> to [[Lorenzo Mascheroni|Mascheroni]] in a 1787 edition of Euler's book ''[[Institutiones calculi differentialis]]''<ref name="N3UF6" /> offered the "justification"

<math display="block">0^0 = (a-a)^{n-n} = \frac{(a-a)^n}{(a-a)^n} = 1</math>

as well as another more involved justification. In the 1830s, [[Guglielmo Libri Carucci dalla Sommaja|Libri]]<ref name="3QtOF" /><ref name="Libri1833" /> published several further arguments attempting to justify the claim {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}, though these were far from convincing, even by standards of rigor at the time.<ref name="Knuth1992" />

===As a limiting form===
Euler, when setting {{math|1=0{{sup|0}} = 1}}, mentioned that consequently the values of the function {{math|0{{sup|''x''}}}} take a "huge jump", from {{math|∞}} for {{math|''x'' < 0}}, to {{math|1}} at {{math|1=''x'' = 0}}, to {{math|0}} for {{math|''x'' > 0}}.<ref name="Euler" /> In 1814, [[Johann Friedrich Pfaff|Pfaff]] used a [[squeeze theorem]] argument to prove that {{math|''x''{{sup|''x''}} → 1}} as {{math|''x'' → 0{{sup|+}}}}.<ref name="Möbius1834" />

On the other hand, in 1821 [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy|Cauchy]]<ref name="PwNOb" /> explained why the limit of {{math|''x''{{sup|''y''}}}} as positive numbers {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} approach {{math|0}} ''while being constrained by some fixed relation'' could be made to assume any value between {{math|0}} and {{math|∞}} by choosing the relation appropriately. He deduced that the limit of the full ''two-variable'' function {{math|''x''{{sup|''y''}}}} without a specified constraint is "indeterminate". With this justification, he listed {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} along with expressions like {{math|{{sfrac|0|0}}}} in a [[Indeterminate form#List of indeterminate forms|table of indeterminate forms]].

Apparently unaware of Cauchy's work, [[August Ferdinand Möbius|Möbius]]<ref name="Möbius1834" /> in 1834, building on Pfaff's argument, claimed incorrectly that {{math|''f''(''x'')<sup>''g''(''x'')</sup> → 1}} whenever {{math|''f''(''x''), ''g''(''x'') → 0}} as {{mvar|x}} approaches a number {{mvar|c}} (presumably {{mvar|f}} is assumed positive away from {{mvar|c}}). Möbius reduced to the case {{math|1=''c'' = 0}}, but then made the mistake of assuming that each of {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}} could be expressed in the form {{math|''Px''{{sup|''n''}}}} for some continuous function {{mvar|P}} not vanishing at {{math|0}} and some nonnegative integer {{mvar|n}}, which is true for analytic functions, but not in general. An anonymous commentator pointed out the unjustified step;<ref name="S" /> then another commentator who signed his name simply as "S" provided the explicit counterexamples {{math|(''e''<sup>−1/''x''</sup>)<sup>''x''</sup> → ''e''{{sup|−1}}}} and {{math|(''e''<sup>−1/''x''</sup>)<sup>2''x''</sup> → ''e''{{sup|−2}}}} as {{math|''x'' → 0{{sup|+}}}} and expressed the situation by writing that "{{math|0{{sup|0}}}} can have many different values".<ref name="S" />

===Current situation===
* Some authors define {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} as {{math|1}} because it simplifies many theorem statements. According to Benson (1999), "The choice whether to define {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} is based on convenience, not on correctness. If we refrain from defining {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}}, then certain assertions become unnecessarily awkward. ... The consensus is to use the definition {{math|1=0<sup>0</sup> = 1}}, although there are textbooks that refrain from defining {{nowrap begin}}{{math|0<sup>0</sup>.}}"<ref name="Benson" />{{nowrap end}} [[Donald Knuth|Knuth]] (1992) contends more strongly that {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} "''has'' to be {{math|1}}"; he draws a distinction between the ''value'' {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}}, which should equal {{math|1}}, and the ''limiting form'' {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} (an abbreviation for a limit of {{math|''f''(''t'')<sup>''g''(''t'')</sup>}} where {{math|''f''(''t''), ''g''(''t'') → 0}}), which is an indeterminate form: "Both Cauchy and Libri were right, but Libri and his defenders did not understand why truth was on their side."<ref name="Knuth1992" />
* Other authors leave {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} undefined because {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} is an indeterminate form.<ref name="vtShl" /><ref name="mfcsT" />

There do not seem to be any authors assigning {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} a specific value other than 1.<ref name="Benson" />

==Treatment on computers==

===IEEE floating-point standard===
The [[IEEE 754-2008]] floating-point standard is used in the design of most floating-point libraries. It recommends a number of operations for computing a power:<ref name="Muller_2010" /> 
*<code>pown</code> (whose exponent is an integer) treats {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} as {{math|1}}; see {{section link||Discrete exponents}}.
*<code>pow</code> (whose intent is to return a non-[[NaN]] result when the exponent is an integer, like <code>pown</code>) treats {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} as {{math|1}}.
*<code>powr</code> treats {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} as NaN (Not-a-Number) due to the indeterminate form; see {{section link||Continuous exponents}}.

The <code>pow</code> variant is inspired by the <code>pow</code> function from [[C99]], mainly for compatibility.<ref name="AFaJ2" /> It is useful mostly for languages with a single power function. The <code>pown</code> and <code>powr</code> variants have been introduced due to conflicting usage of the power functions and the different points of view (as stated above).<ref name="hVrIi" />

===Programming languages===
The C and C++ standards do not specify the result of {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} (a domain error may occur). But for C, as of [[C99]], if the [[normative]] annex&nbsp;F is supported, the result for real floating-point types is required to be {{math|1}} because there are significant applications for which this value is more useful than [[NaN]]<ref name="JJg1b" /> (for instance, with [[#Discrete_exponents|discrete exponents]]); the result on complex types is not specified, even if the informative annex&nbsp;G is supported. The [[Java (programming language)|Java]] [[method (computer science)|method]] <code>java.lang.Math.pow</code>,<ref name="vH81X" /> the [[.NET Framework]] [[method (computer science)|method]] <code>System.Math.Pow</code>,<ref name="DaiDu" /> [[Julia (programming language)|Julia]], and [[Python (programming language)|Python]]<ref name="AGCLB" /><ref name="mbxdz" /> also treat {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}} as {{math|1}}. Some languages document that their exponentiation operation corresponds to the <code>pow</code> function from the [[C mathematical functions|C mathematical library]]; this is the case with [[Lua (programming language)|Lua]]'s <code>^</code> operator<ref name="regQj" /> and [[Perl]]'s <code>**</code> operator<ref name="m5ocl" /> (where it is explicitly mentioned that the result of <code>0**0</code> is platform-dependent).

===Mathematical and scientific software===
[[R (programming language)|R]],<ref name="ijVs7" /> [[SageMath]],<ref name="DIJz1" /> and [[PARI/GP]]<ref name="pari-commit-c2fac9a15" /> evaluate {{math|{{var|x}}{{sup|0}}}} to {{math|1}}. [[Wolfram Mathematica|Mathematica]]<ref name="Wolfram" /> simplifies {{math|{{var|x}}{{sup|0}}}} to {{math|1}} even if no constraints are placed on {{math|{{var|x}}}}; however, if {{math|0{{sup|0}}}} is entered directly, it is treated as an error or indeterminate. [[Wolfram Mathematica|Mathematica]]<ref name="Wolfram" /> and [[PARI/GP]]<ref name="pari-commit-c2fac9a15" /><ref name="5slbi" /> further distinguish between integer and floating-point values: If the exponent is a zero of integer type, they return a {{math|1}} of the type of the base; exponentiation with a floating-point exponent of value zero is treated as undefined, indeterminate or error.

Other such forms are {{math|∞/∞}}, {{math|0 × ∞}}, {{math|∞ − ∞}}, {{math|0<sup>0</sup>}}, {{math|1<sup>∞</sup>}} and {{math|∞<sup>0</sup>}}.}}</ref>
